tldr: Internal cavities inside an object cannot be seen from its outer appearance, but their structure can be inferred from how the object deforms and bounces during a collision. To solve the problem where conventional density-based optimization gets trapped in local minima, this paper proposes a two-stage framework that combines structural hypothesis search with particle-based fine-tuning, achieving highly accurate hidden cavity reconstruction and future dynamic prediction.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method. Starting from a dense particle representation, Stage I selects the best cavity configuration from a global hypothesis space, and Stage II continuously refines the particle positions using differentiable physics simulation.
overview:
For robots to manipulate objects dexterously and for physics simulators to accurately predict future behavior, knowing not just an object's appearance but also whether it has internal cavities and where its mass is concentrated is essential. However, it is impossible to detect internal cavities simply by looking at a static object. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this by inferring hidden interior structures from multiview video observations of a collision event.

Prior SfC methods relied on gradient-based optimization that continuously updates spatial density, but this approach harbors a fundamental trap. When an internal cavity causes an object's post-collision trajectory to drift, gradients trying to match surface motion end up carving away density in completely the wrong place. Furthermore, because a cavity represents a void where no material exists, density gradients inside or near it are extremely weak, causing optimization to stall or diverge.

To overcome this issue, the authors reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning. They treat the cavity location and coarse geometry as discrete hypotheses and explore candidates globally using forward-only physics simulations in Stage I. Then, taking the best-matching hypothesis as an initialization, Stage II refines details at the particle level via continuous optimization with differentiable physics simulation.

Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the density-based baseline in geometric accuracy (lower Chamfer distance) and substantially improves the accuracy of future post-collision dynamics predictions.
contributions: Identified and visualized the fundamental failure mechanism of conventional density-based SfC, where incorrect surface motion gradients and the absence of material lead to severe local minima
Reformulated internal cavity recovery as hypothesis-space reasoning, establishing a framework that handles explicit structural hypotheses
Proposed a two-stage optimization approach combining gradient-free global hypothesis search with local Lagrangian particle refinement via differentiable simulation

Demonstrated superior performance over the baseline in both interior reconstruction accuracy and future dynamic prediction on the SfC benchmark and a topology stress-test dataset with complex internal geometries

sections.heading: Introduction: Revealing Hidden Cavities Through Collisions
sections.summary: Even if two objects look identical on the outside, internal cavities drastically change how they bounce upon impact. Addressing the SfC problem of recovering hidden cavities from multiview collision video, this work proposes a hypothesis-space reasoning approach instead of conventional density optimization.
sections.details:
Computer vision has made great strides in reconstructing 3D shapes from camera video, but these techniques only capture an object's visible surface. However, when a robot grasps or tosses an object, its physical behavior is governed by its internal mass distribution. For instance, two spheres that look identical from the outside will bounce in opposite directions after hitting the floor if one has a cavity on its left side and the other on its right.

Structure from Collision (SfC) tackles this challenge. It attempts to estimate hidden cavities from deformation cues during collisions, but it is an exceptionally difficult inverse problem. Cavities are only observable indirectly through surface motion. Moreover, because voids correspond to regions where material is missing, gradient descent on standard density fields suffers from vanishing gradients and gets easily stuck in local minima.

This paper shifts paradigms by representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses rather than implicit density fields. By decoupling coarse structural exploration in a global stage from continuous particle refinement in a local stage, the method avoids local minima and recovers faithful internal geometry.

sections.heading: Related Work: From Appearance Recovery to Physics and Interior Estimation
sections.summary: 3D reconstruction has progressed from static visual appearance to dynamic deformation, and recently to estimating physical parameters with physics simulators. However, most existing works assume homogeneous interiors, setting them apart from SfC which aims to uncover unknown internal voids.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, three related lines of research are worth reviewing:

- **Static and Dynamic 3D Reconstruction**: Techniques like NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) now enable high-fidelity tracking of visual appearance and surface deformations for both static scenes and dynamic, non-rigid objects. However, they focus exclusively on visible surfaces and remain blind to internal mass distributions.
- **Physics-Informed Modeling**: An increasing number of recent methods embed differentiable simulators into visual reconstruction pipelines to estimate physical properties such as Young's modulus. Yet, most assume objects are solid and homogeneous throughout, leaving them unable to capture variations in internal topology.
- **Structure from Collision (SfC)**: The prior work on recovering hidden cavities from collision behavior, SfC-NeRF, tried to carve out cavities by locally updating voxel densities. Because it relied on local gradients without a structured hypothesis space, it suffered from a critical flaw: it carved cavities in the wrong locations, as analyzed below.

sections.heading: Problem Setup and Why Density Optimization Fails
sections.summary: SfC aims to inversely estimate an object's initial particle state from multiview collision footage. The density-based local gradient approach used in prior work fails structurally because surface motion errors prompt optimization to remove mass on the opposite side of the actual cavity.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Consider calibrated multiview video providing time-varying visible surfaces $\mathcal{S}(t_j)$ and 2D silhouette masks $\mathcal{A}_i(t_j)$. The object is modeled as a continuum using a particle-based representation. Given known material properties $\Theta_{\mathrm{phys}}$ (such as Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio), the goal of SfC is to estimate an initial particle configuration $\hat{\mathcal{P}}(t_1)$ such that the predicted surfaces and masks from a physics simulator (the Material Point Method, or MPM) match actual observations.

### 3.2 Why Does Density-Based Local Optimization Fail?
Figure F2 illustrates the decisive reason. Consider a sphere with a cavity on its left side (a). When dropped onto the floor, its shifted center of mass causes it to bounce to the left (b). Conversely, a solid sphere (c) bounces straight up in simulation (d).

When computing gradients to reconcile this trajectory discrepancy (e), the optimizer tries to make the simulated object tilt further to the left. Astonishingly, it does so by carving away mass from the *right* side of the sphere. In other words, local gradients attempting to align surface motion point in the exact opposite direction of the true cavity on the left.

Furthermore, because a cavity is a void containing no material, density gradient signals inside it are practically nonexistent. Starting from a solid shape, local gradient methods fall prey to incorrect local minima and fail to recover coherent cavity shapes.

captions.F2: The failure mechanism of conventional density-based optimization. When the ground-truth cavity is on the left (a), the observed bounce veers to the left (b). But a solid initial state (c) bounces straight up (d), causing surface gradients to mistakenly carve mass from the right side to close the gap (e).

sections.heading: Proposed Method: Hypothesis-Space Reasoning and Two-Stage Optimization
sections.summary: The proposed framework consists of two stages: Global Hypothesis Optimization, which evaluates low-dimensional explicit cavity hypotheses using forward simulations, and Local Particle Refinement, which polishes particle positions using differentiable simulation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Overall Pipeline
The proposed method starts with a dense particle representation built from observations and optimizes in two stages (Figure F3):

- **Stage I (Global Hypothesis Optimization)**: Evaluates discrete cavity hypotheses using gradient-free, forward-only MPM simulations.
- **Stage II (Local Particle Refinement)**: Uses the best selected hypothesis as an initial state and continuously refines particle positions via gradient descent with differentiable MPM simulations.

### 4.2 Structural Hypothesis Space Design
A cavity hypothesis $h$ is defined by a compact parameter set $h=(\tau, \bm{c}, s, \bm{R})$, representing shape type $\tau$, center $\bm{c}$, size $s$, and orientation $\bm{R}$. A candidate particle configuration $\hat{\mathcal{P}}_h(t_1)$ is generated by carving out particles falling within hypothesis $h$ from the dense particle set. The search space can be customized based on prior knowledge (e.g., searching only position with a fixed size, or selecting from candidate shape templates).

### 4.3 Stage I: Global Hypothesis Optimization
Carving particles for each hypothesis creates discontinuous structural changes, making local gradient descent unsuitable. Therefore, a gradient-free search, such as a coarse-to-fine grid search (defaulting to 250 total simulations), is employed.
The evaluation metric is the 2D mask loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{2D}}$ restricted to frames around the impact, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{col}}$. Focusing purely on the plausibility of motion right around the collision is a clever design that avoids penalizing early unrefined hypotheses for long-term simulation drift.

### 4.4 Stage II: Local Lagrangian Particle Refinement
Once the best hypothesis $h^*$ is identified, initial particle coordinates are directly optimized over all frames $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{all}}$ ($N=14$ frames) using differentiable MPM. The objective combines a 3D surface Chamfer distance loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}$ with the 2D mask loss.

Additionally, two geometric regularizers are introduced: a repulsion loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}$ to prevent unnatural particle clustering, and a volume preservation loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}$ to maintain particle volume during deformation. These ensure smooth surfaces without destroying the underlying cavity topology established in the global stage.

captions.F3: Workflow of the proposed method: (0) Construct a dense particle representation, (I) generate hypotheses and select the best structure via forward simulation evaluated on collision-frame masks, and (II) refine detailed particle positions via differentiable simulation with geometric regularizations.

sections.heading: Experiments: How Accurately Can Unknown Cavities Be Recovered?
sections.summary: On the SfC benchmark, the proposed method substantially outperforms the SfC-NeRF baseline in reconstruction and prediction accuracy. It exhibits particularly strong advantages on cavity location variation tasks, where local gradients typically lose their way.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on the SfC benchmark, which contains 40 sequences spanning 5 outer geometries (sphere, cube, bicone, cylinder, diamond) with varying cavity sizes and positions, as well as a Topology dataset featuring 60 configurations with complex internal voids. Metrics include Chamfer distance (CD, lower is better, displayed as $10^3 \times$ in tables) and F-score (higher is better) against ground-truth particles, alongside rendered image quality (PSNR / SSIM) on future frames.

### 5.2 Benchmark Reconstruction Performance
Compared to the SfC-NeRF baseline, the proposed method achieved superior performance across both size-variation and position-variation settings. In the position-variation task in particular, while SfC-NeRF got trapped in local minima and yielded fractured, unnatural internal cavities, the proposed method recovered clean, coherent cavities closely matching ground truth (Figure F4). This demonstrates that global search successfully captures correct spatial arrangements without being misled by surface errors.

### 5.3 Ablation Studies
Testing each component on the position-variation task revealed that adding global search dramatically improved CD compared to a naive visual-hull hollowed initialization, and local refinement yielded the best overall geometric accuracy. The results also confirmed that both repulsion and volume preservation losses are crucial for particle stability.

### 5.4 Topology Stress Tests and Future Prediction
When tested on intricate cavities (such as snowman and triple-tunnel shapes), fully unconstrained reconstruction with only size priors showed limitations. However, providing a hypothesis space that selects from candidate templates significantly boosted accuracy. Furthermore, in future frame prediction (+7 and +14 frames after observation), the proposed method's accurate interior geometry clearly outperformed both a homogeneous baseline (GIC) and SfC-NeRF in PSNR and SSIM.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison on the diamond geometry under cavity position variation. SfC-NeRF (c) creates fragmented interiors and its post-collision motion deviates from observations, while the proposed method (d) recovers a clean cavity, with ablations (e–g) showing progressive improvements across stages.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work: Moving Toward Real-World Application
sections.summary: This study relies on synthetic simulation data, leaving real-world noise and modeling discrepancies for future work. Additionally, autonomously discovering arbitrary, highly complex topologies that lie outside the hypothesis space remains challenging.
sections.details:
The authors candidly outline several limitations:

- **Real-World Data and Simulation Gap**: The experiments assume synthetic data with perfectly calibrated cameras and an exact match between the simulator's material model and reality. Although robustness tests under motion blur and reduced frame rates succeeded, handling real camera noise and contact friction discrepancies (the Sim-to-Real gap) remains an open challenge.
- **Difficulty in Discovering Arbitrary Topologies**: Relying solely on indirect collision cues to infer intricate internal topologies without prior assumptions is physically under-constrained (ill-posed). Structures absent from the hypothesis space (such as multiple disjoint voids) cannot be captured during the global stage, and local refinement cannot induce topological changes to create them.

Future directions include incorporating learned shape priors and extending internal estimation to everyday manipulation actions such as squeezing or shaking objects.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Unlocking Hidden Structures from Collision Dynamics
sections.summary: This study exposes the fundamental flaw of density-based gradients in SfC and establishes hypothesis-space reasoning as a viable alternative. By coupling physics simulation with geometric optimization, it provides a solid foundation for inferring invisible interior structures from physical phenomena.
sections.details:
Addressing the intuitive yet formidable problem of figuring out what is inside an object by watching it bump into things, this paper offers an elegant solution.

Its analysis clearly explains why conventional density optimization fails, and its division of labor—screening coarse structural hypotheses globally and refining particle details with differentiable simulation—is neatly designed. When robots encounter unknown objects, being able to tap or drop them to gauge internal mass distribution before executing precision manipulation or simulation marks an important milestone toward advanced robotic intelligence.

takeaways: Absence of material (voids) easily causes density gradients to get stuck in local minima, making low-dimensional discrete hypothesis search remarkably effective.

Decoupling coarse structural search (gradient-free forward simulation) from detailed geometric tuning (differentiable simulation) achieves both computational efficiency and high reconstruction fidelity.

Relying solely on surface motion errors can mislead optimization into carving mass on the opposite side due to center-of-mass shifts, making collision-frame masking in global evaluation indispensable.
Accurately recovering internal mass distribution fundamentally dictates the precision of long-term physical dynamics prediction in robotics and digital twins.
limitations: Validation is limited to fully controlled synthetic environments (simulation videos), leaving real-world camera calibration errors and physical model mismatches untested.
Completely unknown topologies outside the predefined hypothesis space (such as numerous tiny cavities or complex porous networks) cannot be discovered autonomously.
Computational cost in the global search phase scales exponentially with hypothesis space dimensionality, requiring advanced sampling strategies if parameter counts increase.
